t: The People’s Charter of 1838 asked for six reforms: a vote for every man over twenty-one, the secret ballot, no property qualification for MPs, payment of MPs, equal constituencies and annual elections.

Petitions signed by 1.3 million people in 1839 and over three million in 1842 were rejected by the House of Commons, and the risings and strikes that followed were put down with arrests and transportation.
Chartism directly won no reform, but its demands were enacted later by other reformers: the secret ballot in 1872, payment of MPs in 1911 and full manhood suffrage in 1918.
dyk: In 2011 a small pamphlet of 16 hymns, previously unknown and uncatalogued, was discovered in Todmorden Library; it is believed to be the only Chartist hymnal in existence.
ev: The People’s Charter is published, setting out the movement’s six aims
A petition signed by 1.3 million working people is presented to the House of Commons, which votes not to hear the petitioners
John Frost leads several thousand marchers to the Westgate Hotel in Newport, where more than twenty Chartists are killed
A second petition of over three million signatures is rejected, and a wave of strikes spreads from the Staffordshire Potteries
Feargus O’Connor is elected for Nottingham, the only Chartist ever to become an MP
A peaceful mass meeting on Kennington Common sends the third petition to Parliament, while 100,000 special constables stand by
The final National Convention is attended by only a handful of delegates

f.where: the United Kingdom, strongest in Northern England, the East Midlands, the Staffordshire Potteries, the Black Country and the South Wales Valleys; meetings in London, Birmingham, Glasgow and Manchester; smaller groups in Ireland and Scotland; later an influence in Australia
f.period: launched 1838; first petition and Newport Rising 1839; second petition and strike wave 1842; National Land Company 1844–1848; third petition and Kennington Common meeting 1848; decline in the 1850s, last National Convention 1858
f.figures: Feargus O’Connor, owner of the Northern Star and its best-loved leader; William Lovett of the London Working Men’s Association; John Frost, leader of the Newport Rising; George Julian Harney, editor and advocate of physical force; Ernest Jones, barrister and socialist; Thomas Cooper, poet
f.outcome: all three petitions rejected and the movement suppressed; after it faded, five of its six points became law between 1867 and 1918, all but annual elections
